summaries.example: Imagine watching a mystery movie for the second time. You already know who took the treasure, but you may still worry while the detective searches. One idea says you are pretending, for a little while, that the answer is not settled. Another says the suspense comes from wanting to help but being unable to change what happens.
summaries.summary: The paradox of suspense is a puzzle about stories we watch more than once. Usually, suspense seems to involve uncertainty: we worry about a bad result, hope for a good one, and do not know which will happen. But when we remember a movie’s ending, the uncertainty seems gone. Still, viewers often report feeling some suspense again. The entry examines four possible explanations. The first says that real uncertainty is not needed; imagining an outcome as open can be enough. The second says suspense comes from a frustrated wish to affect an important event, even when we know its result. The third says viewers may not be able to use their memory of the ending while deeply caught up in the story. The fourth says viewers may call fear, anxiety, or anticipation “suspense” by mistake. Each idea has difficulties. For example, suspense can sometimes grow during a second viewing because viewers notice danger signs they missed before. The entry also separates suspense from surprise and points out that a full theory should explain why suspense often fades with repeated watching.
key_ideas: Many people think suspense needs uncertainty, fear, and hope.
The puzzle is that a story can still feel suspenseful even when we already know its ending.
One answer says we imagine the ending as still open while we watch.
Another answer says suspense comes from wanting to affect what happens but having no power to do so.
Other answers say we briefly fail to use our memory of the ending, or that we mistake another feeling for suspense.
Suspense often becomes weaker after many viewings, and a good theory should explain that too.
summaries.why_it_matters: This puzzle helps us think carefully about emotions, memory, imagination, and stories. It shows that watching a movie is not only about knowing facts. Our feelings may also depend on what we imagine, want, notice, and can or cannot change. Thinking about suspense can help us ask better questions about why books, movies, games, and other stories affect us.

important_terms.definition: A feeling of worry and excitement about what will happen next, especially when something important is at stake.
Not knowing which possible result will happen.
A feeling of being pulled toward a result while being unable to make it happen.
A problem made from ideas that seem to disagree with one another.

questions_to_think_about: Can you feel worried during a story even when you know the characters will be safe?
Is pretending that an ending is unknown enough to create suspense?
How is suspense different from simply waiting for something to happen?
Why might a story show new clues when you watch it again?

summaries.example: Suppose you rewatch a thriller whose protagonist you know will survive. During a scene in which an antagonist approaches, you may still feel fear and an urge to intervene, even though the outcome is certain. The entertained-uncertainty view says you imaginatively treat the outcome as open. The desire-frustration view says your wish to influence the scene is blocked because fiction gives you no real agency. A critic might instead say you feel anticipation or anxiety, not suspense proper. The competing explanations interpret the same reported experience in different ways.
summaries.summary: The entry investigates the paradox of suspense: if suspense requires uncertainty, why can familiar narratives remain suspenseful when their outcomes are known? A standard account treats suspense as a combination of fear about an undesirable prospect, hope for a desirable prospect, and uncertainty concerning which prospect will occur. It also suggests that suspense depends on the stakes and their perceived likelihood. Four proposed solutions revise different parts of the paradox. Noël Carroll’s entertained-uncertainty view claims that fictional engagement allows viewers to imagine an outcome as unsettled without genuinely believing it is unsettled. Aaron Smuts’s desire-frustration theory rejects uncertainty as necessary and locates suspense in the partial frustration of a desire to influence an imminent event; fictional spectators are powerless to intervene. Richard Gerrig’s moment-by-moment forgetting theory retains uncertainty but argues that remembered outcomes are not effectively available during immersion. Robert Yanal’s emotional misidentification view denies that a true repeater feels suspense, proposing that anticipation or another emotion is mislabeled. The entry raises objections to each. Rewatching can reduce suspense, but it can also increase it by making earlier clues newly significant. This creates pressure for any theory to explain both phenomena. Finally, suspense and surprise are distinguished: surprise involves an expectation being overturned, whereas suspense need not involve surprise and need not depend on uncertainty in the same way.
key_ideas: The standard account links suspense to fear, hope, uncertainty, and the importance of the stakes.

The paradox consists of three claims that appear individually plausible but conflict together: suspense requires uncertainty, knowing an ending removes uncertainty, and repeat viewers can still feel suspense.
The entertained-uncertainty and desire-frustration theories reject the claim that actual uncertainty is required.
The moment-by-moment forgetting theory keeps uncertainty as necessary but challenges the claim that remembered outcomes always remove it.
The emotional misidentification theory keeps uncertainty as necessary and challenges reports that familiar narratives produce genuine suspense.
A satisfactory theory must also explain diminishing suspense after repeated viewings and the unusual power of fictional narratives to create suspense.
summaries.why_it_matters: The paradox matters because it connects philosophical questions about emotion with ordinary experiences of film, literature, and games. It asks whether emotions depend on beliefs, imagined possibilities, desires, memory, or the structure of an event. It also illustrates a broader philosophical method: when several plausible claims conflict, a theory must identify which claim to revise and explain the evidence that remains. The discussion cautions against assuming that a familiar label, such as “suspense,” automatically settles what a viewer is feeling.

important_terms.definition: A composite emotional response involving fear of an undesirable outcome, hope for a desirable one, and, on the standard account, uncertainty about which outcome will occur.
A cognitive condition in which one does not know which possible outcome will occur; the standard account treats it as necessary for suspense.
The view that suspense needs only uncertainty entertained in imagination, rather than genuine uncertainty about the story’s result.
The theory that suspense results when a desire to affect an imminent event is partly blocked or frustrated.
The proposal that viewers who know a story’s ending temporarily fail to use that knowledge while the narrative unfolds.
The view that repeat viewers misclassify fear, anxiety, or anticipation as suspense because genuine suspense requires uncertainty.
A response caused by an expectation being suddenly overturned; it is not the same as uncertainty.

questions_to_think_about: If you know a character survives, can your fear for that character still count as suspense? What would make it so?
Does being unable to affect a fictional event explain suspense better than imagined uncertainty?
How could a theory explain both renewed attention to clues and weaker suspense during rewatching?
Why should surprise and suspense be analyzed separately?
Are viewers reliable judges of their own emotional states?

summaries.example: You replay a mystery game and remember that the bridge will hold. Even so, as your character walks toward it, you may feel nervous. You cannot change the game’s recorded story, and you may imagine that the bridge could still fail. A friend might say this is suspense. Another might say it is only anticipation, because you already know the result. The disagreement is about what suspense really requires, not just about whether your reaction feels strong.
summaries.summary: The paradox of suspense concerns a familiar experience: a movie or game can remain suspenseful after we learn its ending. The usual account says suspense combines fear about a bad possibility, hope for a good possibility, and uncertainty about what will happen. It also suggests that suspense grows when the stakes are important. Rewatching creates a problem because remembered knowledge seems to remove uncertainty, yet viewers often still react strongly. The entry discusses four answers. The entertained-uncertainty theory says viewers can imagine the result as undecided even while knowing the actual ending. The desire-frustration theory says uncertainty is not essential; suspense comes from wanting to influence an approaching event while being partly unable to do so. In a film, the audience cannot warn a character or alter the plot. The moment-by-moment forgetting theory says people remain uncertain because their memory of the ending is not effectively used during immersion. The emotional misidentification theory takes the opposite approach: it says genuine suspense requires uncertainty, so repeat viewers are probably feeling anticipation, anxiety, or fear and giving it the wrong name. The entry also discusses difficulties for all four views. A theory must account for the common decline of suspense across viewings, but also for cases where a second viewing makes hidden warning signs more noticeable and a scene more tense. Surprise is separate because it comes from an expectation being overturned, not simply from failing to know the outcome.
key_ideas: The standard explanation says suspense involves fear of a bad outcome, hope for a good outcome, and uncertainty about which will happen.
The paradox appears when a person remembers a story’s ending but still reports suspense during a replay.
The four theories solve the puzzle by rejecting different parts of the three-part argument.
Some theories say actual uncertainty is unnecessary; another says remembered knowledge is temporarily unavailable; another questions the report that repeat viewers feel suspense.
Repeated viewing can lower suspense, but knowing the ending can also reveal clues that make a scene feel more intense.
Suspense and surprise can occur together, but they are different responses.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic shows how philosophy can begin with an everyday puzzle and use it to examine complicated ideas about emotions and the mind. It helps explain why knowing a plot is not always the same as becoming emotionally detached from it. It also teaches us to compare explanations: a theory should fit ordinary reports, distinguish related feelings, and explain both increased and decreased reactions on repeated encounters with a story.

important_terms.definition: Worry and excitement about an important event whose result seems not fully settled.
A state of not knowing which possible result will occur.
The puzzle created when a set of ideas seems reasonable one by one but cannot all be true together.
A view that says imagining an outcome as undecided can produce suspense, even when you know the actual ending.
A view that explains suspense through a blocked wish to influence an upcoming event.
A view that says people may temporarily fail to bring a known ending to mind while absorbed in a story.
A view that says repeat viewers may confuse anticipation, fear, or anxiety with genuine suspense.
The feeling caused when something happens differently from what you expected; it is related to, but not identical with, suspense.

questions_to_think_about: Does imagining that an ending could be different create real uncertainty or only pretend uncertainty?
Can wanting to help a character explain suspense when you know you cannot affect the story?
Why might a second viewing make one scene less suspenseful but another scene more suspenseful?
How could you tell suspense apart from anticipation?
Should a theory trust what viewers say they feel?
